pages.text:
*Days without rain: 120 (until tonight).*

The cloud above the shrine did not sit. It boiled and churned, a grey-green mess that looked like water trying to escape a pot. Yun’s long body trembled beneath it, the mist wrapping around him like a scarf he was afraid to remove. Under his chin, the pearl glowed with a heavy, white light that seemed to hum.

Mei stood in the center of the yard. Her hands shook, but her feet stayed planted on the dirt. She looked up at the dragon, then around at the waiting village. She did not ask for permission. She counted. One. Two. Three. Four.

She raised her voice. It was not a whisper. It was a clear, steady note.

"Out for four."

Beside her, Tao lifted his wooden drumstick. Hua raised her hand, her fingers stiff but ready. Nainai’s bamboo stick thumped once on the ground, a sharp, solid sound. The man with the spoon lowered his hands from his ears. He lifted the spoon instead. The air held its breath.
pages.image: Yun, one single terrified sea-green dragon, trembles high above the stone shrine in a swirling grey storm cloud, while below in the yard Mei holds her ground, Tao lifts a drumstick, and Nainai thumps her bamboo stick on the dirt, villagers gathered around at dusk.

pages.text:
Yun opened his mouth.

The sound that came out was not a bang. It was a roll. It started low, deep in his chest, and then it climbed. It rolled across the terraces, down the valley, and back up the mountain. It rattled the tiles on the roofs and shook the pots hanging in the kitchens. Every hair on every head stood up.

It was enormous. It was joyful.

It felt like the whole sky clearing its throat. It felt like a giant laughing. The sound did not hurt. It did not scare. It hummed warm against the skin, the way a bee hums near a flower, but much, much bigger. It was the sound of a door opening. The sound of a long silence breaking. It was the most beautiful noise Mei had ever heard.
pages.image: Yun, the sea-green dragon, high above the village rooftops with his mouth open in a great joyful roar, big golden ripples of sound spreading out over the tile roofs, villagers below looking up in wonder with delighted smiles at dusk.

pages.text:
For a second, the village was silent.

Then Uncle Shi lifted his steel thermos and banged it against the stone shrine. *Clang.*

The school drum boomed. *Boom.*

Pots from every window clanged together. Spoons rattled on bowls. Children shouted, their voices high and bright. Old Grey, the water buffalo, looked up and rang his small brass bell. *Ding.*

Uncle Shi’s eyes were wet. Tears ran down his round cheeks. He shouted, "We are here!"

And a hundred voices shouted it back.

"We are here!"

The sound went up to the cloud. It went up to the dragon. Yun’s whiskers stood straight out. His amber eyes were wide. He looked less like a creature of the sky and more like a boy who had just been told he was not alone.
pages.image: A village of villagers in a muddy yard shouts together, banging pots and drums. A large grey water buffalo rings a brass bell, and a sea-green dragon hovers above, his whiskers standing straight out in astonishment.

pages.text:
The first drop hit the red dust. It made a tiny dark star in the dirt, right next to Tao’s boot.

Then ten. Then a hundred. The smell rose up from the ground. It was warm and dusty and sweet, like the inside of a cupboard that has been shut too long. It was the smell of earth breathing out. It was the smell of rice leaves uncurling. It was the end of the long, dry wait.

Tao did not hesitate. He stomped into the first puddle. His yellow rain boots splashed with a loud *thwup*.

"Yes!" he shouted, his face bright. "Finally useful!"

He jumped again. The water soaked the green tiger on his shirt, but he did not care. He was laughing. The rain came down on the terraces, on the cracked stream bed, on the upturned faces of the village. It was cold, and it was wet, and it was perfect.
pages.image: Tao alone, in his bright yellow rain boots and green tiger T-shirt, stomps joyfully into a big puddle in a muddy village lane, water splashing up, soft rain falling on green terraced fields behind him.

pages.text:
Nainai walked to the center of the yard. Her knees were stiff, but her back was straight. She lifted her face to the rain. She closed her eyes. She laughed. It was a short, bright laugh, the kind a girl uses when she is surprised by a gift.

She took the bamboo stick out of her jacket. She held it up to the light. Then, very solemnly, she put it back. She cut no notch.

"Water finds a way," she said softly.

Mei stood in the rain, soaked to the skin. She was shaking with cold and joy. She looked up at the dragon, who was hovering close, his pearl dimming as the rain filled the air.

"Thank you, Yun," Mei said. It was the biggest sentence she had ever said.

Overhead, softly, a dragon answered.

"Thank you, Mei."
pages.image: An elderly woman with grey hair in a bun stands in the rain, laughing with her face upturned, while a small girl in a blue jacket looks up at a gentle sea-green dragon hovering above, both figures illuminated by the falling rain.
